extracted.intended_audience: readers, potential subscribers, contributors and advertisers of The Forerunner (interested in social reform, women's issues, and progressive domestic/childcare ideas)
extracted.subtask_description: Front-matter and essays from The Forerunner that set out the magazine's purpose, content and advertising policies, and that advance prescriptive standards for child-culture, domestic organization, and the qualities of good historical/essay writing. Useful for understanding editorial criteria and social-policy prescriptions tied to creative-writing and publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of good historical writing (Ida Tarbell appraisal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The historian's power to collate facts and so marshall them as to give a clear picture of the time and scenes in question; a strong, far-seeing mind at work; the direct style; and the value of the subject matter place such a writer high among our present day teachers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the attributes by which the author praises and ranks a historical writer; deviation from such standards (e.g., sentimentalizing or mischaracterizing 'society') is grounds for criticism. Example: the author admires Tarbell for these qualities but is disappointed when Tarbell's March essay presents unconvincing claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magazine purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The Forerunner is 'to stimulate thought: to arouse hope, courage and impatience; to offer practical suggestions and solutions, to voice the strong assurance of better living, here, now, in our own hands to make.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content should aim to provoke constructive thought and practical improvement in everyday life; the magazine's tone and selection should support social betterment and actionable ideas rather than mere entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magazine content scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishes 'stories short and serial, article and essay; drama, verse, satire and sermon; dialogue, fable and fantasy, comment and review.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors will include a wide variety of literary forms and genres; each issue should contain fiction, essays, verse, drama and critical material consistent with the magazine's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Forerunner is 'written entirely by Charlotte Perkins Gilman.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All editorial voice and content direction derive from a single authorial perspective; contributors/sections should reflect the central author's viewpoints and aims (in this case, C.P. Gilman's).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological stance / thematic focus
rubrics_metrics.description: The Forerunner 'is a magazine for humanity, and humanity is social. It holds that Socialism, the economic theory, is part of our gradual Socialization, and that the duty of conscious humanity is to promote Socialization.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions and editorial choices should be compatible with or explicitly engage the magazine's commitment to socialization/social reform; pieces should address people, principles, and everyday public and private problems through that lens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising policy — personal-knowledge endorsements
rubrics_metrics.description: In its advertising department will be described articles personally known and used. So far as individual experience and approval carry weight, and clear truthful description command attention, the advertising pages of The Forerunner will be useful to both dealer and buyer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertised products should be presented through personal experience and truthful description; the magazine will publish advertisers' own statements only if it believes them to be true. Emphasis on honesty and usefulness over puffery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents and value proposition for subscribers
rubrics_metrics.description: A year's subscription will provide: one complete novel by C.P. Gilman, one new book by C.P. Gilman, twelve short stories, twelve-and-more short articles, twelve-and-more new poems, twelve short sermons, plus departments such as Comment and Review and Personal Problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subscription pricing and marketing should be justified by enumerated content offerings; pricing communicated clearly ($1.00 a year; .10 a copy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal Problems department scope and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The department's purpose is 'to seriously discuss real "personal problems" such as do arise in most lives; and to which neither the minister nor Ruth Ashmore do justice.' It is not proposed to furnish absolute wisdom; only comparative. The department does not discuss etiquette, fashions or the removal of freckles. Foolish questions will not be answered, unless at peril of the asker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions submitted must be substantive and serious; trivial or purely social/etiquette questions are excluded. Replies aim to be practical and comparative rather than absolute moralizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Childcare institution standards (baby-houses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Places for babies to spend part of the day away from their mothers—'beautiful, comfortable, hygienic, safe and sweet and near—one for every twenty or thirty families perhaps'—staffed not by casual apprentices but by 'Genius, Training and Experience' (a nurse-mother, a teacher-mother, a Human Mother).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Childcare facilities should be high-quality, local, and staffed by experienced, specially trained caregivers (not inexperienced nurses); they should gather factual knowledge of childculture to 'teach the mothers' and raise standards across families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion of kindergarten/day-nursery model
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocate multiplying kindergartens and day-nurseries 'a thousand fold'—making them beautiful, hygienic, safe, and placing expert care to allow mothers to learn and take home new knowledge and standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale and professionalize early childhood education so that community-level accumulation of expertise can improve child-rearing practices; day care becomes a vehicle for maternal education and the development of child-culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic organization via specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Housekeeping should be specialized: 'Workshops. The Cleaning Establishment, the Laundry--the Cookshop; the Service Bureau; each and all in charge of its Genius--its special person who likes that kind of work and does it well.' Homes should be 'kitchenless' and serviced by skilled cleaners and prepared food delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply specialization and professional organization to domestic labor to improve sanitary standards, economy, comfort and to free individuals to work in roles for which they have aptitude; reduce drudgery and raise overall living standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for a 'real home'
rubrics_metrics.description: Every family should have 'a real home, with a real garden' that is 'quiet, sweet and kitchenless'—a place of peace, comfort, joy and pride, seclusion, mutual companionship, rest, beautiful privacy and rest—not a workshop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Home design and services should prioritize rest, companionship and beauty; household systems should relieve occupants of menial burdens so home can fulfill these ideals for both men and women.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of 'Genius' in domestic and maternal tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be Domestic Genius and Mother-Genius—people who love and do domestic or maternal work well; their expertise will lift the whole world forward by improving health, brain-power, peace of mind and standards of child-rearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify, cultivate and deploy individuals who are exceptionally skilled and passionate about domestic and child-rearing work rather than relying on unskilled average labor; value specialization and training over the expectation that all will 'do their own work' equally well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of motherhood vs housework
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern woman's dread often stems not from child-bearing but from the 'life-long task of child-rearing' and the burden of housework for which she feels unfit; children need Genius in detailed services and education; 'Better one well-born and well-trained, than the incapable six survivors of the unnecessary twelve.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and cultural responses should acknowledge women's reluctance as rational and focus on improving systems of child-rearing and household management (training, specialization, institutional support) rather than moralizing or coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversation as medium of civilization versus mere 'society'
rubrics_metrics.description: True exchange of ideals and service occurs in conversation; 'It is through society that the quickening of mind and heart best comes about... It is the very foundation of civilization... Ideas find life or death there.' But 'society' as a round of amusements often fails to produce such conversation and quickening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish superficial social entertainment from meaningful conversational exchange; value gatherings that foster thoughtful discussion and exchange of ideals over mere frivolous amusements. Critique of treating social life solely as entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for measurable standards in domestic competence
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'not even a standard whereby to judge our shortcomings' in housekeeping; the lack of known better practices prevents improvement—society lacks standards for domestic skill and childculture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop, collect and disseminate factual knowledge and standards (via expert baby-houses, training, and specialized services) so households can be judged and improved against real standards rather than custom and habit.
